what_its_for: Docetaxel is a chemotherapy medicine used to treat several types of cancer, including breast cancer, lung cancer, prostate cancer, stomach cancer, and head and neck cancer. It works by stopping cancer cells from growing and dividing.
how_to_take: Docetaxel is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion directly into your vein at a hospital or cancer treatment center. A nurse or doctor will administer it for you — you cannot take this medicine at home on your own. Each infusion usually takes about 1 hour. Before each treatment, you will be given steroid pills (usually dexamethasone) starting the day before your infusion to help prevent allergic reactions and reduce swelling. Take those steroid pills exactly as your doctor tells you.
dosing: Your doctor will calculate your exact dose based on your body size (height and weight), the type of cancer being treated, and how well you are tolerating treatment. Treatments are usually given once every 3 weeks, but your schedule may be different. Always follow your cancer care team's instructions for your specific treatment plan.
missed_dose: Because docetaxel is given by a healthcare professional at a clinic or hospital, it is very important that you keep all of your scheduled appointments. If you need to cancel or reschedule an appointment, call your doctor or treatment center right away. Do not try to reschedule on your own without talking to your care team first, as timing of chemotherapy is very important.
storage: Docetaxel is stored and prepared by trained pharmacists and nurses at your treatment center. You do not need to store this medicine at home. If you are given steroid pills (like dexamethasone) to take before your treatment, store those at room temperature away from heat, moisture, and direct light, and keep them out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid contact with people who are sick or have infections, as chemotherapy weakens your immune system and makes it easier for you to get sick. Do not receive any live vaccines (such as nasal flu spray) while on treatment without talking to your doctor first. Avoid drinking alcohol unless your doctor says it is okay. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for some time after. Use effective birth control during treatment and for a period after, as docetaxel can harm an unborn baby. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and protect your skin, as your skin may become more sensitive.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: a fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher (this can be a sign of serious infection); chills, shaking, or signs of infection; severe allergic reactions such as sudden rash, hives, difficulty breathing, chest tightness, or swelling of the face or throat (these can happen during the infusion); unusual bruising or bleeding; swelling of your hands, feet, or legs; severe diarrhea or vomiting; numbness, tingling, or burning in your hands or feet; mouth sores that make it hard to eat or drink; extreme tiredness or weakness; shortness of breath; or any new or worsening symptoms that concern you.
when_it_works: Docetaxel starts working right away at the cellular level, but it may take several treatment cycles before you or your doctor can see or measure results. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular lab tests and imaging scans. Everyone responds differently to chemotherapy, so be patient and stay in close contact with your care team.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Docetaxel can cause serious harm or death to an unborn baby. Do not use if you are pregnant. Use effective contraception during treatment and for several months after the last dose. Tell your doctor immediately if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed while receiving docetaxel and for some time after your last dose. Talk to your doctor about when it may be safe to resume breastfeeding. Older adults (65+): Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects such as infections, mouth sores, and skin reactions. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Liver problems: Docetaxel is processed by the liver. If you have liver disease or elevated liver enzymes, your dose may need to be adjusted or treatment may not be appropriate. Your doctor will check your liver function before and during treatment. Children: The safety and effectiveness of docetaxel in children have not been well established for most uses.
